record.original_question: Given a polynomial Diophantine equation P(x1, ..., xn) = 0 with integer coefficients, determine whether its set of integer solutions is a finite union of polynomial families, where a polynomial family means a subset S of Z^n for which there exist polynomials P1, ..., Pn in integer parameters u1, ..., uk such that (x1, ..., xn) belongs to S exactly when xi = Pi(u1, ..., uk) for all i.

evidence.quote: Definition 1. Let Zn be the set of vectors (x1, . . . , xn) with integer coordinates xi. We say that a subset S subseteq Zn is a polynomial family if there exist an integer k >= 0 and polynomials P1, . . . , Pn in k variables u1, . . . , uk with integer coefficients such that (x1, . . . , xn) in S if and only if there exist integers u1, . . . , uk such that xi = Pi(u1, . . . , uk), i = 1, . . . , n.
Problem 1. Given a polynomial Diophantine equation (1), determine whether the set of its integer solutions is a finite unions of polynomial families.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let n be a positive integer and let Z^n denote the set of n-tuples of integers. A subset S ⊆ Z^n is called a polynomial family if there exist a non-negative integer k and polynomials P_1, …, P_n ∈ Z[u_1, …, u_k] (with integer coefficients) such that
  S = { (P_1(u_1,…,u_k), …, P_n(u_1,…,u_k)) : (u_1,…,u_k) ∈ Z^k }.
Equivalently, (x_1,…,x_n) ∈ S if and only if there exist integers u_1,…,u_k with x_i = P_i(u_1,…,u_k) for every i = 1,…,n.

Problem. Provide an algorithm (or prove that no algorithm exists) which, given as input a polynomial P(x_1,…,x_n) ∈ Z[x_1,…,x_n], decides whether the set
  V_Z(P) := { (x_1,…,x_n) ∈ Z^n : P(x_1,…,x_n) = 0 }
of integer solutions of the Diophantine equation P(x_1,…,x_n) = 0 can be expressed as a finite union of polynomial families in the sense above.
artifact.status_search_result: The decision problem of whether the integer solution set of a general polynomial Diophantine equation admits a finite polynomial parametrization appears open. Polynomial parametrizations are known in special cases (genus 0 equations, SL_2(Z), Pythagorean triples, certain norm forms via results of Frisch–Vaserstein and Vaserstein), but no general decision procedure is known, and Hilbert's 10th problem (Matiyasevich, 1970) shows the broader solvability question is undecidable, suggesting this refinement is at least very hard.

status_evidence.title: Polynomial parametrization for the solutions of Diophantine equations and arithmetic groups
status_evidence.snippet: A polynomial parametrization for the group of integer 2x2 matrices with determinant one is given, solving a problem of Skolem and Beukers; many Diophantine equations are shown to admit polynomial parametrizations of integer solutions.
status_evidence.claim: Polynomial parametrizations are known in important special cases but not in general.

status_evidence.title: Polynomial parametrization of the solutions of Diophantine equations of genus 0
status_evidence.snippet: For Diophantine equations of genus 0, all integral solutions can be parametrized by a single triple of integer-valued polynomials.
status_evidence.claim: Genus 0 case is solved; higher genus / general case remains open.

status_evidence.title: Hilbert's tenth problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: There is no algorithm which, for a given arbitrary Diophantine equation, decides whether the equation has a solution in integers (Matiyasevich, 1970).
status_evidence.claim: The companion solvability question is undecidable, indicating this parametrization decision problem is highly nontrivial.
